Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
Between Us is a visual system for translating social interactions into visual systems. The project began by asking whether something as subjective as communication could be reduced to a set of rules. I identified four variables within an interaction: understanding, engagement, avoidance, and success, and used them to control the direction, distance, movement, and eventual meeting point of lines traveling between two individuals.

Early experiments isolated these interactions one at a time. Two circles represented two people, while animated lines moved toward one another. Depending on the conditions assigned to the interaction, the lines could meet, overlap, pass one another, or move in different directions. Randomness was built into the system so that similar conditions could produce related, but never identical, outcomes.

As the project developed, I became more interested in what happened when these individual exchanges accumulated in a specific place over a set period of time, as a way to archive a social gathering. The final iteration records multiple interactions occurring within the same space and period of time. Each colored circle represents an individual, with the number of lines emerging from it determined by how many interactions that person had. Some become highly connected, while others remain more isolated. Each trajectory retains the variables of the original system, while the dotted lines were added to represent the "missed opportunity" of an interaction -- how much understanding was lost, how much avoidance can redirect one's path, and the visual space that's left as a result.

Rather than trying to objectively measure human communication, the system uses code to reduce highly complex and subjective human patterns into simplified forms.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This system models the physical assembly and the many possibilities of studio ceramics through visual rules. Each vessel is assembled along a central axis from three stacked components - a base, midsection, and neck - selected from randomized geometric shapes and bounded sizes, ensuring the base remains the structural foundation. 

Surface appearances translate simulated physical and atmospheric conditions: clay body determines opacity (40% Porcelain, 70% Stoneware, 100% Terracotta), while glaze chemistry responds to kiln oxygen levels. Cobalt produces a constant deep blue, Copper shifts from an oxidized green-turquoise gradient to a reduced deep red, and Iron Oxide transforms from a warm yellow-brown gradient to charcoal. 

By combining and controlling the variables within this system, across 32 geometric profiles, 18 material states, and continuous component scaling, the system generates infinite unique, visually readable ceramic pots that can be helpful to the ceramicist when reading the appearance.

Your Project Name: A week Daily Sleep Quality Data
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
7Days is an algorithmic data translation system that transforms personal, tracked sleep logs from Monday through Sunday into an expressive visual cipher. Developed through an integrated workflow bridging computational code in p5.js and Adobe Illustrator, the system treats daily bio metric quality as dynamic parameters rather than passive static records.

Moving beyond conventional health charts that flatten personal metrics, 7Days reclaims bio metric tracking as an active generator of form, texture, and structural meaning. Operating within p5.js, the system maps sleep metrics—including total duration, REM/deep sleep ratios, heart rate variability (HRV), and wake frequencies—to geometric parameters: deep sleep drives smooth, low-frequency wave functions, REM generates high-frequency node clusters, frequent awakenings introduce sharp spatial noise and fractures, and HRV governs the organic fluidity of the vector field.

The rendered SVG geometry is subsequently imported into Adobe Illustrator for vector refinement, where paths are enhanced with custom variable-width brushes, precision alignment, and chromatic hierarchy, deep indigo's represent restorative deep sleep, soft purples denote REM cycles, and high-contrast neon accents mark sleep interruptions. Arranged sequentially across a master seven-day grid, the final piece translates intimate biological rhythms into a cohesive weekly narrative that seamlessly bridges data art and computational design.
File 1 description: The system programmatically evaluates sleep quality and duration based on input variables. Each geometric cipher functions as a clock face, where the dashed contour outlines the exact time and duration of sleep.
File 2 description: I used if and else if statements to dynamically control the visual output based on daily sleep quality.
File 3 description: In p5.js, the design rules dynamically convert sleep logs into visual geometry, sleep deficit triggers push(), rotate(), and vertex() to build 90-degree rotated orange polygons (Need More Sleep), overlaid with line() vectors radiating outward to create sharp spike-like tension.

Your Project Name: PLOT TWIST: A Competitive Storytelling Game
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
PLOT TWIST is a competitive storytelling game where two writers create different stories from the same seven prompts. The game uses seven variable categories: genre, protagonist, desire, conflict, setting, relationship, and twist, each with multiple possible values. Each round, a Director selects three prompts, and the two Writers each select two prompts from the remaining categories. Together, these seven prompts form one shared setup. Both Writers then have three minutes to use the same setup to create a title and one-sentence description for an original television show.

The Writers pitch their stories to the Director, who chooses the winning interpretation. The winner earns one point, the Director role rotates, and the next round begins. The first player to reach five points wins. Through playtesting, the system produced five rounds, ten different television shows, and five winning outcomes, demonstrating how the same set of prompts can lead to very different stories depending on how each player interprets and combines them.

Your Project Name: BECOMING A MICROSCOPE TO CREATE NEW SECRETS
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
BECOMING A MICROSCOPE TO CREATE NEW SECRETS

This project begins with an everyday object: my phone. I chose five words—anxious, communicative, connective, dependent, and navigable—to explore how it shapes my daily life. A phone helps me communicate, maintain relationships, and find my way, but it can also create anxiety and dependence. I wanted to translate these overlapping feelings into a visual language.

Over five weeks, I developed symbols through drawing, digital translation, sequencing, elimination, and chance. Each stage changed how I understood the original forms. Instead of illustrating a phone directly, I explored how shapes could suggest its emotional and social roles. Using four actions drawn from Richard Serra’s Verb List—tightening, joining, layering, and mapping—I transformed five selected forms into twenty graphic experiments.

The title describes a way of looking closely. “Becoming a microscope” means paying attention to relationships and details that I usually overlook. “Creating new secrets” means allowing familiar ideas to become unfamiliar symbols, open to different interpretations.

Built with HTML, CSS, and p5.js, the website documents the process in the order it developed. It brings the experiments together so viewers can follow how a word becomes a shape and how that shape changes through a set of rules. The project explores how observation and repeated transformation can turn an ordinary object into a personal visual system.

Your Project Name: Map as Medium: Deconstructed Navigational Storytelling
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara: I approached this project with the goal of questioning what a map can be, what it can do, and what stories it can tell. Maps are generally designed to be used in reference to a physical space or pathway(s), so I wanted to explore how I could deconstruct the map as a pre-existing system, and find new ways of visualizing map-generated pathways. I presented my participants with a basic map of Cobble Hill, Brooklyn, along with a prompt: "You are in this neighborhood from 10am to 10pm. Plot out your pathway on the provided map, circling any establishments/buildings you enter." They were welcome to go places not explicitly labeled, as long as it was within the drawn boundaries. I visualized each pathway by first filling in the overall shape; then presenting only the outline of the pathway; and finally by straightening out each path into one line, placing a dot where a building was entered, and a slash where a corner was turned. I also layered all the pathways on top of each other to get an idea of what blocks/areas were most heavily trafficked by my users.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
Phase 1 explores "Rules, Variables, and Systems," asking: What happens when visual form is not authored as a static outcome, but emerges dynamically from an autonomous rule set?

"Organic Recursion: Simulating Avian Self-Organization within an Algorithmic Atmospheric Field" is an interactive generative system built in p5.js. The concept originated by comparing two decentralized systems: starling murmurations in nature, where birds follow local neighbors to produce collective waves, and Taiwan’s waste grid, where trucks broadcast classical music to choreograph daily routines. Both revealed that technology is an organized schedule and shared rhythm. Before coding, I tested these mechanics physically using an aluminum tray, paperclips, and magnets, discovering how magnetic fields drive alignment and physical barriers force flow to bifurcate.

In the computational system, 160 typographic particle agents navigate an open 1200x800 canvas. Grounded in Craig Reynolds’ steering behaviors (separation, alignment, cohesion), Karl Gerstner’s programmatic matrices, and Casey Reas’s environmental variables, agents negotiate between flocking instincts and external stresses. Rather than drawing literal birds, each agent is an abstract typographic mark resembling movable type.

The system runs on an autonomous 20-second loop across four phases:

Stochastic Dispersion (0–5s): High separation scatters agents in Brownian wandering.

Directional Stream Flow (5–10s): Peak alignment locks agents into parallel migratory waves.

Localized Vortex Swirls (10–15s): Cohesion and torque fracture the flock into rotating sub-swarms.

Stochastic Organic Gathering (15–20s): Dynamic attractors pull agents into a porous typographic cluster.

Interactive perturbations include stochastic crosswinds up to 60 knots sonified live via Web Audio pink noise ([W], [M]), cartographic contour obstacles with a hydrodynamic tangential bifurcation algorithm ([J], [C]), and an entropic predator hawk ([H]).
